chunks: "A ground plane is a continuous layer of copper dedicated to ground, usually right under the signal layers, that acts as the reference and the return path for everything above it.
The pros: it's very low impedance, so it keeps the ground voltage nearly the same everywhere and avoids shared-impedance noise from ground traces.
At high frequency the return current flows directly under each signal trace, so the loop is small, which means less radiation, less pickup and less crosstalk.
It makes controlled impedance possible, because a microstrip or stripline needs a reference plane.
It shields signals on one side of the plane from the other, it spreads heat, and next to a power plane it adds distributed capacitance for decoupling.
The cons: it costs layers, so money.
It adds parasitic capacitance to anything near it, which matters for high-impedance nodes or fast analog and RF circuits, so I sometimes cut it away under those.
It can still carry noise: if a noisy current flows through the plane near a sensitive circuit, they share impedance.
If you cut slots or splits into it, the return path breaks and it makes things worse. A big plane pair can resonate.
And big planes make soldering harder, which is why you use thermal reliefs on pads. So I use it by default, and I'm careful where I interrupt it."
